questions.clue: A numerical outcome whose possible values form a countable set.
questions.explanation: The possible values can be listed, even if the list has no end.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 356, Random variable

questions.clue: A numerical outcome that can take any value in an interval, such as a measurement before rounding.
questions.explanation: A density assigns probabilities to intervals of possible values.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 102, Continuous variable

questions.clue: A function that gives the probability of each individual value of a discrete variable.
questions.explanation: Its values are point probabilities, and they sum to one.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 338, Probability distribution

questions.clue: A nonnegative function whose area over an interval gives its probability.
questions.explanation: Integrating the density over a range gives the chance of landing in that range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 338, Probability density

questions.clue: A function giving the chance that a random variable does not exceed a specified value.
questions.explanation: For each cutoff x, it returns the probability that X is at most x.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 117, Cumulative distribution function. Uses the at-most convention from MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: A variable coded 1 when an event occurs and 0 otherwise.
questions.explanation: Its numerical value records whether the specified event happened.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 216, Indicator variable

questions.clue: Record 1 if a single coin toss is heads and 0 otherwise. What is the model for the recorded value?
questions.explanation: A single binary trial with fixed success probability follows a Bernoulli model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 42, Bernoulli distribution

questions.clue: Count heads in 20 independent tosses of the same coin, with a fixed chance of heads.
questions.explanation: This counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials with a common success chance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution

questions.clue: Calls arrive one at a time, independently, at a steady rate. What models the hourly count?
questions.explanation: The event count in a fixed period of a homogeneous Poisson process has a Poisson distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson distribution

questions.clue: Toss the same coin independently until the first head. Record the total tosses.
questions.explanation: The geometric model describes trials to the first success under independent trials with constant success probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 186, Geometric distribution
questions.convention: Counts the successful trial, so the smallest value is 1.

questions.clue: Draw five cards from a shuffled deck without replacement. Count the aces.
questions.explanation: Sampling without replacement from a fixed population leads to a hypergeometric count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 211, Hypergeometric distribution

questions.clue: A wheel’s landing angle has equal probability in every arc of the same length.
questions.explanation: A continuous uniform model has constant density on its range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 441, Uniform distribution

questions.clue:
Σₓ x · P(X = x)
for a discrete X
questions.explanation: The expected value weights each possible outcome by its probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 156, Expected value
questions.math_clue:
$\sum_x x\,P(X=x)$
for a discrete $X$

questions.clue:
E[(X − μ)²]
where μ = E[X]
questions.explanation: Variance measures the expected squared distance from the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{E}[(X-\mu)^2]$
where $\mu=\mathrm{E}[X]$

questions.clue:
σ / √n
for n independent draws with standard deviation σ
questions.explanation: Averaging n independent draws divides their standard deviation by the square root of n.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}$
for $n$ independent draws with standard deviation $\sigma$
questions.math_explanation: Averaging $n$ independent draws divides their standard deviation by the square root of $n$.

questions.clue:
X / n
where X is the number of successes in n trials
questions.explanation: The proportion is the observed number of successes divided by the total trial count.
questions.reference: UC Berkeley STAT 2, Fall 2024, Module 7, sample percentage: https://stat2.berkeley.edu/fall-2024/#module-7-sampling-from-a-population-weeks-11-12
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{X}{n}$
where $X$ is the number of successes in $n$ trials

questions.clue:
(x − μ) / σ
where μ and σ are population values
questions.explanation: This gives the number of population standard deviations from the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard scores
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$
where $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are population values

questions.clue:
F(b) − F(a)
for a cumulative distribution function F and a < b
questions.explanation: Subtracting the cumulative probabilities gives P(a < X ≤ b).
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b, Cumulative Distribution Function: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/
questions.math_clue:
$F(b)-F(a)$
for a cumulative distribution function $F$ and $a < b$
questions.math_explanation: Subtracting the cumulative probabilities gives $P(a<X\leq b)$.

questions.clue: The probability distribution of a statistic across repeated samples of a fixed size.
questions.explanation: The variable here is the statistic, such as a sample mean, rather than an individual measurement.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: Differences in a statistic that arise when equal-sized random samples are drawn from one population.
questions.explanation: Different random samples can give different values of the same statistic.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling variation

questions.clue: Learning the outcomes of earlier draws leaves the probability law for the next draw unchanged.
questions.explanation: Earlier outcomes carry no information about the next draw when the draws are independent.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 3, §6: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_class03-prep.pdf

questions.clue: What theorem gives a normal limit for standardized means of independent draws from one finite-variance population?
questions.explanation: This theorem concerns the shape of the standardized sampling distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: As independent draws accumulate, their average approaches the population mean, when the mean exists.
questions.explanation: The law concerns the location of the average as the sample grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 244, Law of large numbers

questions.clue: Using a bell-shaped model for averages of large independent samples from a skewed, finite-variance population.
questions.explanation: For large samples, the central limit theorem makes the normal model a useful approximation for the sample mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation. Sample mean case in MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: Measure the wait from now until the first arrival of a constant-rate Poisson process.
questions.explanation: The continuous wait to the next event is exponential under this process.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution

questions.clue: Measure the time to the fourth arrival in a constant-rate Poisson process.
questions.explanation: A sum of four independent exponential waits with a common rate has a gamma distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 179, Gamma distribution
questions.convention: Shape 4, with rate equal to the arrival rate. The scale is its reciprocal.

questions.clue: A positive variable becomes normally distributed after taking its natural logarithm.
questions.explanation: The normality applies to the log of the variable itself.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 259, Lognormal distribution

questions.clue: Gaussian sensor readings are rescaled to have mean zero and variance one. What is the resulting distribution?
questions.explanation: A normal distribution with mean zero and variance one is standard normal.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard normal variable

questions.clue: Toss the same coin independently. Count tails before the fourth head.
questions.explanation: For independent tosses with a fixed success probability, the failure count before a fixed number of successes follows a negative binomial model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 298, Negative binomial distribution
questions.convention: Counts failures before the fixed success count.

questions.clue: A probability p varies across machines with density proportional to p(1 − p) for 0 < p < 1.
questions.explanation: The density is a beta model with both shape parameters equal to two.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 43, Beta distribution
questions.math_clue:
A probability varies across machines. Its density is proportional to the following expression on the indicated support.
$p(1-p),\quad 0<p<1$

questions.clue:
√[(N − n) / (N − 1)]
for n draws without replacement from N > 1 units
questions.explanation: This factor shrinks the standard error relative to drawing with replacement.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 166, Finite population correction
questions.convention: Here the population variance uses denominator N and the correction multiplies the standard error.
questions.math_clue:
$\sqrt{\frac{N-n}{N-1}}$
for $n$ draws without replacement from $N > 1$ units

questions.clue: E[(X − μₓ)(Y − μᵧ)]
questions.explanation: Covariance averages the product of the centered variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 110, Covariance
questions.math_clue: $\mathrm{E}[(X-\mu_x)(Y-\mu_y)]$

questions.clue:
Cov(X, Y) / (σₓσᵧ)
with positive standard deviations
questions.explanation: Pearson correlation is covariance scaled by the two standard deviations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 107, Correlation coefficient
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)}{\sigma_x\sigma_y}$
with positive standard deviations

questions.clue:
Σᵧ P(X = x, Y = y)
for discrete X and Y
questions.explanation: Summing over Y gives the probability that X takes the specified value.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 267, Marginal distribution
questions.math_clue:
$\sum_y P(X=x,Y=y)$
for discrete $X$ and $Y$

questions.clue:
P(X = x, Y = y) / P(Y = y)
with a positive denominator
questions.explanation: The ratio gives the chance that X equals x within the group where Y equals y.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 98, Conditional distribution
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{P(X=x,Y=y)}{P(Y=y)}$
with a positive denominator

questions.clue:
1 − F(t)
where F(t) = P(T ≤ t) and T is time to an event
questions.explanation: The survival function gives the chance that the event happens after t.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 423, Survival function
questions.math_clue:
$1-F(t)$
where $F(t)=P(T\leq t)$ and $T$ is time to an event

questions.clue: Independent readings are normally distributed. What describes the sample mean’s distribution, even with only four readings?
questions.explanation: The mean of independent normal readings is itself exactly normal.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 26, §26.1, Sums of Independent Normal Random Variables: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson26

questions.clue: A computer picks eight distinct employees so that every possible group of eight has the same chance.
questions.explanation: A simple random sample without replacement makes all size-eight subsets equally likely.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 394, Simple random sampling

questions.clue:
E[exp(tX)]
where this expectation exists around t = 0
questions.explanation: Taking the expectation of the exponential gives the moment generating function.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 282, Moment generating function
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{E}[\exp(tX)]$
where this expectation exists around $t = 0$

questions.clue:
Var(X) + Var(Y)
for independent X and Y with finite variances
questions.explanation: Independence makes the covariance zero, so the variances add.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 7b, Covariance and Correlation, variance of a sum: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class07-prep-b_pdf/
questions.math_clue:
$\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)$
for independent $X$ and $Y$ with finite variances

questions.clue: A fixed numerical feature of the entire population, such as its true proportion of left-handed people.
questions.explanation: A population parameter describes the population supplying the sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 317, Parameter

questions.clue: A numerical summary calculated from sample data alone, without unknown population quantities.
questions.explanation: A statistic is a function of the observed sample, such as its mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 411, Statistic

questions.clue: A cutoff at or below which a specified percentage of a continuous distribution falls.
questions.explanation: A percentile translates a cumulative percentage into a value on the measurement scale.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 323, Percentile

questions.clue: The list used to identify the units from which a sample can actually be drawn.
questions.explanation: The frame is the operational list, which can differ from the target population.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 100, Lesson 2, Sampling Methods: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson02

questions.clue: A fair ten-sided die has one face for each integer from 0 to 9. What models the number shown?
questions.explanation: Each of the ten discrete results has the same probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 441, Uniform distribution

questions.clue: A library splits its branches by region and randomly samples branches from every region.
questions.explanation: The regions are strata, and every stratum contributes to the sample.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 100, Lesson 2, Sampling Methods: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson02

questions.clue: A library randomly selects two branches and surveys every staff member at both.
questions.explanation: The branches are clusters, and all people in selected clusters are included.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 87, Cluster sampling

questions.clue: From a list, a pollster picks a random start among the first ten entries, then takes every tenth entry.
questions.explanation: A random start followed by a fixed interval defines systematic sampling.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 100, Lesson 2, Sampling Methods: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat100/Lesson02

questions.clue:
aE[X] + b
when a and b are constants and Y = aX + b
questions.explanation: Multiplying values multiplies their mean, and adding a fixed amount shifts it.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Problem Set 4 Solutions, affine transformations: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_pset04_sol.pdf
questions.math_clue:
$a\,\mathrm{E}[X]+b$
when $a$ and $b$ are constants and $Y = aX + b$

questions.clue:
a² Var(X)
for Y = aX + b, with a and b fixed
questions.explanation: Adding b shifts the center; multiplying by a scales the variance by a squared.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Problem Set 4 Solutions, affine transformations: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/mit18_05_s22_pset04_sol.pdf
questions.math_clue:
$a^2\mathrm{Var}(X)$
for $Y = aX + b$, with $a$ and $b$ fixed
questions.math_explanation: Adding $b$ shifts the center; multiplying by $a$ scales the variance by $a^2$.

questions.clue:
np
for X counting successes in n independent trials with fixed success chance p
choices: Standard deviation of a binomial count
questions.explanation: The count is a sum of n variables whose individual means are p.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution
questions.math_clue:
$np$
for $X$ counting successes in $n$ independent trials with fixed success chance $p$
questions.math_explanation: The count is a sum of $n$ variables whose individual means are $p$.

questions.clue:
p(1 − p)
for X equal to 1 with probability p and 0 otherwise
questions.explanation: The variance of a single indicator is p times one minus p.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 42, Bernoulli distribution
questions.math_clue:
$p(1-p)$
for $X$ equal to 1 with probability $p$ and 0 otherwise

questions.clue: One probability model describes two random variables together, including how their values occur in combination.
questions.explanation: The joint distribution retains information about the relationship between the variables.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 229, Joint distribution

questions.clue: In a distribution with a finite third moment, the average cubed deviation from the mean is positive.
questions.explanation: Cubing retains the sign of deviations, so large positive deviations can dominate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 397, Skewness

questions.clue: The standardized fourth central moment minus the corresponding value for a normal distribution.
questions.explanation: A normal distribution has kurtosis of three, so its excess kurtosis is zero.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 239, Kurtosis
questions.convention: Excess kurtosis uses normal as the zero reference.

questions.clue: Repeatedly drawing same-size samples with replacement from the observed data to approximate a statistic’s sampling behavior.
questions.explanation: The nonparametric bootstrap uses the observed sample as a stand-in for the population.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bootstrap

questions.clue: For every fixed positive tolerance, the chance of an estimator missing its limit by more than that tolerance tends to zero.
questions.explanation: This mode of convergence controls the probability of deviations from the limit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 104, Convergence in probability

questions.clue: What inequality bounds tails for any distribution with finite variance using only distance from the mean in standard deviation units?
questions.explanation: The upper bound for being at least k standard deviations away is 1/k², with positive variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 77, Chebyshev’s inequality
questions.math_explanation: The upper bound for being at least $k$ standard deviations away is $\frac{1}{k^2}$, with positive variance.

questions.clue: Forty independent voters each pick one of three candidates with fixed probabilities. Model the three counts jointly.
questions.explanation: A multinomial model counts several possible categories across a fixed number of independent trials.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 290, Multinomial distribution

questions.clue: A researcher adds the squares of four independent standard normal values.
questions.explanation: The sum of four independent squared standard normal variables has four chi-squared degrees of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 79, Chi-squared distribution

questions.clue: A lab divides one standard normal reading by another independent standard normal reading.
questions.explanation: The ratio of independent standard normal variables follows the standard Cauchy model.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Cauchy distribution Ratio example in University of Minnesota STAT 3701, Statistical Models, Part II: https://www.stat.umn.edu/geyer/3701/notes/models2.html

questions.clue: A newly started machine has a constant failure rate, and its time to failure is continuous.
questions.explanation: A constant hazard in continuous time leads to an exponential lifetime.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution

questions.clue: As many independent fair-coin tosses accumulate, the proportion of heads stays close to one half with high probability.
questions.explanation: For indicators of heads, the sample mean is the head proportion, and its target is one half.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 244, Law of large numbers

questions.clue: Repair times are right-skewed. For repeated groups of 200 independent repairs, standardized average times have a bell-shaped distribution. Which theorem explains this?
questions.explanation: Independent draws with finite positive variance produce a normal limiting shape after standardization.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue:
exp(−λ) λᵏ / k!
for counts k = 0, 1, 2, …
questions.explanation: The Poisson count law uses a positive expected count λ.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson distribution
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\exp(-\lambda)\,\lambda^k}{k!}$
for counts $k=0,1,2,\ldots$
questions.math_explanation: The Poisson count law uses a positive expected count $\lambda$.

questions.clue:
λ exp(−λx)
for x ≥ 0 and λ > 0
questions.explanation: The exponential density decays from λ at rate λ.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution
questions.convention: λ is the rate, with mean 1/λ.
questions.math_clue:
$\lambda\exp(-\lambda x)$
for $x\geq0$ and $\lambda>0$
questions.math_explanation: The exponential density decays from $\lambda$ at rate $\lambda$.

questions.clue:
np(1 − p)
for a count X from n independent binary trials with success chance p
questions.explanation: The count sums n independent indicators, each with variance p times one minus p.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution
questions.math_clue:
$np(1-p)$
for a count $X$ from $n$ independent binary trials with success chance $p$
questions.math_explanation: The count sums $n$ independent indicators, each with variance $p(1-p)$.

questions.clue:
√[p(1 − p) / n]
for n independent trials with true success chance p
choices: Standard deviation of a binary outcome
Standard error of the success count
questions.explanation: The spread of the sample proportion is the spread of its count divided by n.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 500, Lesson 4, §4.2, Sampling Distribution of the Sample Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/Lesson04
questions.math_clue:
$\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}$
for $n$ independent trials with true success chance $p$

questions.clue: E[X⁴], when finite
questions.explanation: A raw moment uses powers of X itself, without centering.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 282, Moments
questions.math_clue: $\mathrm{E}[X^4]$, when finite

questions.clue: E[(X − E[X])²]
questions.explanation: A central moment uses deviations around the mean; the second one equals variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 282, Moments
questions.math_clue: $\mathrm{E}[(X-\mathrm{E}[X])^2]$

questions.clue: Their joint probability can be written as the product of the two marginal probabilities for every pair of sets.
questions.explanation: Independence requires the factorization for every pair of events defined by the variables.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 7a, Joint Distributions and Independence: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class07-prep-a_pdf/

questions.clue: What describes two variables with finite positive variances when their centered product has expectation zero?
questions.explanation: Zero covariance gives zero Pearson correlation, even if dependence remains.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 107, Correlation coefficient

questions.clue: A bell curve approximates P̂ from independent binary draws when expected success and failure counts are both large.
questions.explanation: A sample proportion is an average of binary indicators; its large-sample shape is approximately normal.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 500, Lesson 4, §4.2, Sampling Distribution of the Sample Proportion: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat500/Lesson04
questions.math_clue:
$\hat P$
A bell curve approximates this proportion from independent binary draws when expected success and failure counts are both large.

questions.clue: When using a continuous approximation for an integer count, move an inclusive upper integer cutoff up by one half.
questions.explanation: The half-unit change includes the whole bar for the last qualifying integer.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation See the half-unit correction in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 28: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson28

questions.clue: Divide a standard normal value by √(V/8), where V is independent chi-squared with eight degrees of freedom.
questions.explanation: This ratio follows Student’s t with degrees of freedom inherited from the chi-squared term.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Student’s t-distribution Ratio definition in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 26, §26.4: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson26
questions.math_clue:
$\sqrt{V/8}$
Divide a standard normal value by this quantity, where $V$ is independent chi-squared with eight degrees of freedom.
questions.math_explanation: This ratio follows Student’s $t$ with degrees of freedom inherited from the chi-squared term.

questions.clue: A factory checks thousands of independent parts, each with a tiny defect probability. Which model can approximate the defect count using its mean alone?
questions.explanation: A binomial count with many trials and small success probability can be approximated by a Poisson count.
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 12, The Poisson Distribution: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson12

questions.clue: Averages of independent Cauchy observations remain Cauchy. Which usual central-limit condition fails?
questions.explanation: The Cauchy distribution has no finite variance, so the elementary normal limit theorem does not apply.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Cauchy distribution

questions.clue: A sensor repeats the same reading 500 times. Which issue defeats an independent-draw central limit argument?
questions.explanation: Copying one observation creates perfectly dependent values, not 500 independent observations.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b, Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue:
√n · (X̄ − μ) / σ
for an independent sample with common mean μ and positive finite SD σ
questions.explanation: Subtract the population mean and divide by the standard error of the sample mean.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b, Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/
questions.math_clue:
$\sqrt{n}\,\frac{\bar X-\mu}{\sigma}$
for an independent sample with common mean $\mu$ and positive finite SD $\sigma$

questions.clue:
σ² / n
for n independent draws from one distribution with variance σ²
questions.explanation: The variance of the sum is nσ², and scaling by 1/n divides variance by n².
questions.reference: Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 24, Several Independent Random Variables: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson24
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{\sigma^2}{n}$
for $n$ independent draws from one distribution with variance $\sigma^2$
questions.math_explanation: The variance of the sum is $n\sigma^2$, and scaling by $\frac{1}{n}$ divides variance by $n^2$.

questions.clue: Var(X) + Var(Y) + 2 Cov(X, Y)
questions.explanation: Dependence can add or subtract from variance through the covariance term.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 7b, Covariance and Correlation: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class07-prep-b_pdf/
questions.math_clue: $\mathrm{Var}(X)+\mathrm{Var}(Y)+2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X,Y)$

questions.clue:
dF(x)/dx
for a differentiable cumulative distribution function F
questions.explanation: The derivative of the CDF gives the density where the derivative exists.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b, Continuous Random Variables: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/
questions.math_clue:
$\frac{dF(x)}{dx}$
for a differentiable cumulative distribution function $F$

questions.clue:
P(X ≥ a) ≤ E[X] / a
for nonnegative X with finite mean and a > 0
questions.explanation: Nonnegative values above a contribute at least a times their probability to the mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 270, Markov inequality
questions.math_clue:
$P(X\geq a)\leq\frac{\mathrm{E}[X]}{a}$
for nonnegative $X$ with finite mean and $a > 0$
questions.math_explanation: Nonnegative values above $a$ contribute at least $a$ times their probability to the mean.

questions.clue:
N(nμ, nσ²)
for the total of many independent draws from one nonnormal population
questions.explanation: Adding n observations scales the mean and variance by n, and the central limit theorem supplies the shape.
questions.reference: MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 6b, Central Limit Theorem and the Law of Large Numbers: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class06-prep-b_pdf/
questions.convention: N(mean, variance). Population mean μ and finite positive variance σ².
questions.math_clue:
$N(n\mu,n\sigma^2)$
for the total of many independent draws from one nonnormal population
questions.math_explanation: Adding $n$ observations scales the mean and variance by $n$, and the central limit theorem supplies the shape.

questions.clue: A worksheet proposes point probabilities for all possible values of a discrete variable. Which requirement checks whether the list accounts for every possible outcome?
choices: They must have a unique maximum
questions.explanation: The point masses exhaust the sample space, which has probability one.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 338, Probability distribution

questions.clue: An insurer models a payout with several possible amounts. What determines the contribution of an amount to the expected payout?
choices: Its distance from the median only
Its distance from the largest payout only
questions.explanation: Expectation weights each possible payout by its probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 156, Expected value

questions.clue: A measurement equals the same constant on every repeat. What does that imply about its deviations from the mean?
choices: They have a symmetric nonzero spread
questions.explanation: The mean is the same constant as every reading, leaving no deviations.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance

questions.clue: Every daily balance receives the same 20-unit credit. What happens to the variance across days?
questions.explanation: A common shift changes the mean by the same amount and leaves all deviations unchanged.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance

questions.clue:
For a random variable with finite second moment, what do these two terms together describe?
E[X²] − (E[X])²
questions.explanation: Variance equals the second raw moment less the squared first moment.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 445, Variance
questions.math_clue:
For a random variable with finite second moment, what do these two terms together describe?
$\mathrm{E}[X^2]-(\mathrm{E}[X])^2$

questions.clue: Under the at-most convention, what does an upward jump in a cumulative distribution function represent?
choices: Probability concentrated at the jump point
The chance of exceeding the jump point
A change in the upper support limit
questions.answer: Probability concentrated at the jump point
questions.explanation: The CDF includes the probability at the point, while its left limit excludes that probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 117, Cumulative distribution function. Uses the at-most convention from MIT 18.05, Spring 2022, Reading 5b: https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-05-introduction-to-probability-and-statistics-spring-2022/resources/mit18_05_s22_class05-prep-b_pdf/

questions.clue: What population quantity does the average value of an indicator represent?
choices: The chance that its event occurs
The chance its event does not occur
The odds of its event occurring
The chance of two independent events
questions.answer: The chance that its event occurs
questions.explanation: The value one contributes its event probability to the mean, and zero contributes nothing.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 216, Indicator variable

questions.clue: Which property makes a fixed set of trials suitable for a binomial count model?
choices: Independent trials with a different success probability each time
Independent trials with one shared success probability
Trials that stop at a fixed success count
Success counts from a randomly varying number of trials
questions.answer: Independent trials with one shared success probability
questions.explanation: The ordinary binomial model needs a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution

questions.clue: Under the convention that a geometric variable counts attempts through the first success, which descriptions fit its support?
choices: A fixed finite set of integers
questions.explanation: Each possible value is a whole attempt count starting at the first attempt.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 186, Geometric distribution

questions.clue: Why does knowing the number of red tiles initially in a box constrain the support of the red count in a sample without replacement?
choices: The sample cannot contain more red tiles than the box holds
Each draw restores the stock of red tiles
Every permitted red count has the same probability
The red count is always the number of draws
The support depends only on the number of blue tiles drawn
questions.answer: The sample cannot contain more red tiles than the box holds
questions.explanation: Without replacement, the finite stock of each colour bounds how many of that colour can be selected.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 211, Hypergeometric distribution

questions.clue: In a homogeneous Poisson process, what two quantities determine the mean event count over an observation window?
choices: The event rate and the start time only
The window length and the first recorded event only
The event rate and the population size
The event rate and the window length
The event rate and the last recorded event only
questions.answer: The event rate and the window length
questions.explanation: The mean count is the rate multiplied by the elapsed time.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson distribution

questions.clue: Which feature lets you compare probabilities of two subintervals under a continuous uniform law?
questions.explanation: A constant density makes interval probability proportional to length.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 441, Uniform distribution

questions.clue: Which statement describes the symmetry of a standard normal distribution?
choices: The two sides of its centre are mirror images
Its longer tail is to the right
Its longer tail is to the left
questions.answer: The two sides of its centre are mirror images
questions.explanation: Reflecting the standard normal curve around its mean preserves its shape.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard normal variable

questions.clue: A homogeneous Poisson process is observed from time zero. Which law describes the waiting time until its fourth event?
questions.explanation: The sum of four independent exponential waiting times has a gamma law.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 179, Gamma distribution

questions.clue: In a multinomial model for a fixed number of parcels with exactly one destination each, why are the destination counts constrained?
choices: Together they exhaust the total number of parcels
They all have the same observed count
questions.answer: Together they exhaust the total number of parcels
questions.explanation: Each parcel contributes to exactly one destination, so their counts have a fixed sum.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 290, Multinomial distribution

questions.clue: A Bernoulli variable equals one on a successful trial. How can the complementary Bernoulli variable be described?
choices: It equals one on every trial
It counts failures until the first success
It counts successes over repeated trials
questions.explanation: Exchanging the labels zero and one records the complement of the original success event.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 42, Bernoulli distribution

questions.clue: In repeated independent trials with one success probability, what distinguishes a negative binomial stopping plan from a fixed-length binomial trial sequence?
choices: The number of successes at stopping is fixed in advance
The total number of trials is fixed in advance
The success probability changes after each trial
Failure can happen only on the final trial
The event of interest is time measured continuously
questions.answer: The number of successes at stopping is fixed in advance
questions.explanation: The negative binomial plan continues until the specified success count is reached.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 298, Negative binomial distribution

questions.clue: A positive measurement is lognormal. Which operation maps the median of its normally distributed log back to the measurement scale?
questions.explanation: The exponential is increasing and reverses the natural logarithm, so it also maps the median back.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 259, Lognormal distribution

questions.clue: Which part of a Poisson model controls both the centre and the spread of its count distribution?
choices: The upper bound on the count
questions.explanation: A Poisson law has one parameter, which specifies both its mean and its variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 330, Poisson distribution

questions.clue: How does the instantaneous failure rate of an exponential lifetime change with age?
questions.explanation: The exponential model has a constant hazard rate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 157, Exponential distribution

questions.clue: Compared with a standard normal, how much probability sits beyond very large cutoffs under a Student t law with 5 degrees of freedom?
choices: More only in the left tail
More only in the right tail
questions.explanation: The t law is symmetric and has heavier tails for finite degrees of freedom.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 419, Student's t-distribution
questions.math_clue: Compared with a standard normal, how much probability sits beyond very large cutoffs under a Student $t$ law with 5 degrees of freedom?
questions.math_explanation: The $t$ law is symmetric and has heavier tails for finite degrees of freedom.

questions.clue: A team repeatedly samples six seeds and records each sample's range. What does the distribution of these ranges approximate?
questions.explanation: Each recorded value is a statistic computed from a different sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: Seed lengths are in centimetres. What are the units of the standard error of their sample mean?
questions.explanation: A standard error is a standard deviation of the statistic and uses the statistic's units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: For independent observations from the same population, how is the standard error of their mean related to the spread of individual observations?
choices: It is the population spread scaled down by the sample size
It is independent of sample size
It is the population spread scaled down by the square root of sample size
It grows in direct proportion to sample size
It grows with the square root of sample size
questions.answer: It is the population spread scaled down by the square root of sample size
questions.explanation: Averaging independent observations reduces their sampling spread at the square-root rate.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: What happens to the standard error of a mean as independent observations from a population with fixed, positive variance are added?
choices: It shrinks by the same amount for each additional observation
It grows with diminishing gains from each additional observation
It stays fixed at the population standard deviation
It shrinks with diminishing gains from each additional observation
It becomes exactly zero as soon as the sample grows
questions.answer: It shrinks with diminishing gains from each additional observation
questions.explanation: Standard error is inversely proportional to the square root of sample size.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: A histogram shows the mean for each of 500 equal-sized samples. What does a single plotted value represent?
questions.explanation: The graph has one statistic per sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: A fixed finite population is measured completely, with no measurement error. Why does the observed mean have no design-based sampling variation?
choices: The individual measurements are all equal
The units were sampled independently with replacement
The population values average to zero
Every census measures all the same population units
questions.answer: Every census measures all the same population units
questions.explanation: Sampling variation comes from which units are observed. A census observes them all.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 166, Finite population correction

questions.clue: When is the finite population correction most relevant to a simple random sample without replacement?
choices: When the sample is a negligible share of the population
When draws are made with replacement
When the sample is a substantial share of the population
When only instrument error is of interest
When the sampling variance is already independent of sample size
questions.answer: When the sample is a substantial share of the population
questions.explanation: Observing a substantial fraction leaves relatively few unobserved units and reduces sampling variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 166, Finite population correction

questions.clue: In simple random sampling without replacement, which objects all have the same selection probability?
choices: All subsets of the fixed sample size
questions.answer: All subsets of the fixed sample size
questions.explanation: Each possible distinct sample of the required size is equally likely.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 394, Simple random sampling

questions.clue: How does an ordinary nonparametric bootstrap choose data for each resample?
choices: Draw without replacement and retain the original sample size
Draw with replacement but always halve the sample size
Draw from a fitted population model at the original sample size
Draw with replacement and retain the original sample size
questions.answer: Draw with replacement and retain the original sample size
questions.explanation: The original dataset serves as the empirical distribution, and the resample matches its size.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bootstrap

questions.clue: Can an original observation be absent from an ordinary bootstrap resample of the same size?
choices: No, each original appears at least twice
Yes, only if the observation is an outlier
Yes, only if the sampling fraction is known
Yes, if other observations are drawn repeatedly
questions.answer: Yes, if other observations are drawn repeatedly
questions.explanation: Sampling with replacement allows some observations to recur and some to be omitted.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bootstrap

questions.clue: A bootstrap produces 1,000 sample medians. Which quantity estimates the median estimator's standard error?
choices: Standard deviation of the starting observations
questions.explanation: The resampled medians approximate the estimator's sampling distribution.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 59, Bootstrap

questions.clue: Two independent random samples give different medians, even though the population and measurement procedure stay fixed. What explains this?
questions.explanation: The samples can contain different members and yield different statistics.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling variation

questions.clue: Two independent-sample means have equal sample sizes. Which mean has greater standard error?
choices: The mean from the population with the higher average
The mean from the less variable population
The mean from the more variable population
The first mean to have been recorded
Neither mean, because equal sample sizes imply equal precision
questions.answer: The mean from the more variable population
questions.explanation: At the same sample size, a greater population standard deviation gives a greater standard error.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: A researcher wants to reduce the standard error of a mean. The population spread and sampling method stay fixed. Which change helps?
choices: Record a duplicate of each existing observation
Shift every observation by the same amount
Sort the same observations before averaging
Change the reporting precision of the final mean
questions.explanation: A larger independent sample reduces the sampling variation of its mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: Three classes are randomly selected and every student in them is surveyed. What was the first-stage sampling unit?
questions.explanation: Whole classes were chosen first, making them the sampled clusters.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 87, Cluster sampling

questions.concept: selection bias versus stable sampling variation
questions.clue: A rental survey samples only advertised properties. If the target is all properties for rent, what problem can persist even with very small standard error?
questions.explanation: Precise results within the listed properties can still miss systematically different unlisted properties.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 386, Selection bias

questions.clue: A recorder adds 5 to every sample mean. How does that affect the standard error across repeated samples?
questions.explanation: A constant shift changes the centre of the sampling distribution but leaves its spread unchanged.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: A larger independent sample reduces the standard error of its mean. Which population property can stay unchanged?
choices: The standard deviation of individual observations
The precision of the sample mean
questions.answer: The standard deviation of individual observations
questions.explanation: Increasing sample size makes the mean more precise even when individual observations remain just as variable.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: Where is the sampling distribution of a mean centred under independent sampling from a population with a finite mean?
choices: At zero regardless of the population
questions.explanation: The sample mean is unbiased for the population mean.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: A program saves the mean and standard deviation from each repeated sample. What determines which sampling distribution a saved value belongs to?
choices: The order in which the sample was taken
The statistic saved from that sample
The result of rounding the sample mean
The name of the underlying population only
The variability across individual observations only
questions.answer: The statistic saved from that sample
questions.explanation: Each statistic has its own distribution over repeated samples.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: What is the relationship between a statistic's standard error and its sampling distribution?
choices: The standard error is its variance
The standard error is its standard deviation
The standard error is its mean
The standard error is its interquartile range
The standard error is its range
questions.answer: The standard error is its standard deviation
questions.explanation: Standard error measures the spread of a statistic in standard-deviation units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 409, Standard error

questions.clue: An analyst plots the heights of the 30 people in one sample. What does this graph show?
choices: The standard error of the mean
The sampling distribution of their mean
The sampling distribution of their median
questions.explanation: The points are individual measurements from a single sample.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 377, Sampling distribution

questions.clue: Individual queue times are right-skewed with finite variance. Under independent sampling, what may become nearly normal as n grows?
choices: The distribution of the observed maximum
The distribution of the queue itself
The distribution of the sample mean
The distribution of each queue time
questions.answer: The distribution of the sample mean
questions.explanation: The CLT concerns the average over repeated samples.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: A histogram of 10,000 independent observations remains right-skewed. Why can the CLT still apply?
choices: It describes the probability of choosing a sample size
It describes a fitted trend line
questions.explanation: The CLT places no requirement on the histogram of individual observations becoming normal.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: To centre and scale a sample mean for a normal approximation, what is subtracted before dividing by the standard error?
questions.explanation: Standardization measures departure from the reference centre in standard-error units.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 410, Standard scores

questions.clue: Why can a normal approximation be poor for a binomial count when successes are expected to be very rare?
choices: The count concentrates near the sample size and is left-skewed
The count has an exactly uniform distribution
The count concentrates near zero and is strongly skewed
questions.answer: The count concentrates near zero and is strongly skewed
questions.explanation: Sparse expected successes leave much of the probability at the lowest few counts.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation

questions.clue: When a continuous curve approximates an integer count, which feature of the cutoff decides the direction of a continuity correction?
choices: Whether the boundary integer is included and which tail is selected
The units used to name the trials
Whether the curve is drawn above the histogram
The order in which trials are observed
questions.answer: Whether the boundary integer is included and which tail is selected
questions.explanation: The corrected region must include exactly the count cells belonging to the event.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation. See the half-unit correction in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 28: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson28
questions.convention: Uses a half-unit continuity correction for integer counts.

questions.clue: For a continuity correction on an inclusive range of integer counts, what happens to the outer boundaries of the approximating interval?
choices: The boundaries both stay at the original integers
questions.explanation: The continuous region must include the full cells at both ends of the count range.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation. See the half-unit correction in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 28: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson28
questions.convention: Uses a half-unit continuity correction for integer counts.

questions.clue: Which source permits an exactly normal distribution of the mean of two independent draws?
questions.explanation: Independent normal variables have normal linear combinations, even at n = 2.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem
questions.math_explanation: Independent normal variables have normal linear combinations, even at $n = 2$.

questions.clue: How does the standard deviation of a sum of independent identically distributed terms grow with the number of terms?
questions.explanation: Independent variances add, and standard deviation is the square root of the sum of variances.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: A sampling distribution is approximated by a normal law. How is probability around its centre distributed?
choices: More probability is above the centre
More probability is below the centre
All probability is at the centre
The answer depends on sample size even under the normal model
The two sides carry equal probability
questions.answer: The two sides carry equal probability
questions.explanation: Any normal law is symmetric about its centre.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: Which population fails the finite-variance condition of the ordinary independent-sample CLT?
questions.explanation: A Cauchy variable has no finite variance.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 70, Cauchy distribution

questions.clue: A program copies one random reading 1,000 times and averages the copies. Why is the independent-sample CLT inapplicable?
choices: The sample mean is always zero
The data have an unknown centre
questions.explanation: Each copy is the same random observation, so the average equals the original draw.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: Which result says an independent sample mean from a finite-variance population gets close to the population mean in probability?
questions.explanation: The law addresses concentration near the mean as sample size grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 244, Law of large numbers

questions.clue: Several independent samples come from the same strongly skewed population with finite variance. How does a much larger sample affect the distribution of the mean?
choices: Its distribution tends toward normality after standardization
The individual observations become normally distributed
Its shape becomes more like the raw population
Its distribution tends toward a uniform shape
The mean no longer varies across samples
questions.answer: Its distribution tends toward normality after standardization
questions.explanation: The central limit theorem describes the standardized sample mean as the sample size grows.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: Which pattern favours a normal approximation to a binomial count?
choices: Expected successes are substantial and failures are almost impossible
Expected failures are substantial and successes are almost impossible
The count is concentrated entirely at zero
The count is concentrated entirely at the sample size
Expected successes and expected failures are both substantial
questions.answer: Expected successes and expected failures are both substantial
questions.explanation: A normal approximation works better when the count is away from its extreme boundaries.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation

questions.clue: After centring a sample proportion at its null value, what rescaling puts it in approximate standard normal units?
choices: Divide by its null standard error
Multiply by the number of trials
questions.answer: Divide by its null standard error
questions.explanation: Standardization measures the centred proportion in units of its null standard deviation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: As independent sample size increases, how does the unstandardized mean's sampling spread change when the population has finite positive variance?
choices: It first increases then levels off
questions.explanation: The mean's standard deviation is inversely proportional to the square root of n.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: What distribution is the classical normal limit for the population-centred sample mean divided by its standard error?
questions.explanation: Centring and dividing by the standard error produce the unit-scale normal limit.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: Which law gives the exact, possibly nonnormal distribution of the sum of 10 independent Bernoulli variables with a common success chance?
questions.explanation: The sum counts successes in a fixed number of independent trials.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 47, Binomial distribution

questions.clue: When approximating the total of many independent identically distributed observations by a normal law, what sets its centre?
choices: The expected value of one typical observation
The variance of one typical observation
The estimated standard error of the sample mean
questions.explanation: The normal approximation for a sum is centred at the sum's own expectation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: What region represents a single attainable integer in a continuity-corrected normal approximation?
choices: Only the half-cell below that integer
Only the half-cell above that integer
The full cell centred on that integer
Every cell up to and including that integer
questions.answer: The full cell centred on that integer
questions.explanation: The normal curve assigns area over the whole cell, whose centre is the original count.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation. See the half-unit correction in Penn State STAT 414, Lesson 28: https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat414/Lesson28
questions.convention: Uses a half-unit continuity correction for integer counts.

questions.clue: An online poll has a nearly normal distribution of means under repeated sampling from its eligible members. What issue remains if members differ from the target population?
choices: The normal centre must equal zero
The standard error must equal the standard deviation
The sampling variance must increase with sample size
The average must take integer values
questions.explanation: Approximate normality does not establish that the sampling population represents the target.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 73, Central limit theorem

questions.clue: A standardized sum of a fixed number of Bernoulli trials closely follows a bell curve. What is the exact sum distribution's type?
questions.explanation: The sum still takes integer values even when a continuous distribution is a good approximation.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 305, Normal approximation

questions.clue: A population has finite variance, but the mean's sampling distribution is poorly approximated by a normal law. Which result still bounds its two-sided tail using variance alone?
questions.explanation: Chebyshev's bound applies to the sampling distribution whenever its variance is finite.
questions.reference: Everitt and Skrondal (2010), 4th ed., p. 77, Chebyshev's inequality
